title: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
summary: Why brute-force nearest-neighbor search stops scaling, how HNSW graphs, IVF cells and product-quantization codes find neighbors fast, how to tune them, and how disk, filters and updates shape production indexes.
outcomes: Explain why brute-force k-NN scales linearly, why trees fail in high dimensions and why LSH needs many tables
Trace greedy and beam (ef) search on a proximity graph and spot a local minimum
Compute HNSW layer sizes and graph memory from M and m_L = 1/ln M
Build an HNSW layer in Python and explain how the neighbor heuristic keeps clustered data connected
Predict IVF cost and boundary misses from nlist and nprobe, and why IVF needs representative training data
Encode vectors with product quantization, estimate distances from a lookup table and recover recall by re-ranking
Tune M, ef_construction and ef against recall@k, and pick HNSW, IVF or PQ for a constraint
Choose disk, rescoring, filtering and update strategies for a production vector index

lessons.title: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling

blocks.md: In the prerequisite course you turned text into embeddings and ranked documents by cosine similarity to a query embedding. That ranking is a **k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) search**: given a query vector $q$ and $N$ stored vectors, return the $k$ vectors closest to $q$ under some distance: Euclidean distance (also called L2 distance, the straight-line length of the difference between two vectors), inner product, or cosine.

The obvious way is **brute force**: compute the distance from $q$ to every stored vector and keep the best $k$. It is exact and simple. Its cost is the problem: every query touches every vector, so the work grows linearly with $N$.

blocks.tex: \text{cost per query} = N \times d \ \text{multiply-adds}, \qquad \text{bytes read} = N \times d \times 4 \ (\text{float32})
blocks.caption: Each distance sums one term per dimension (a multiply-add for a dot product, a subtract and a multiply-add for squared L2), so about d multiply-adds, repeated for all N vectors; each dimension is a 4-byte float32. Brute force reads every stored vector once per query.

blocks.md: Put in real sizes. Ten million documents embedded in 768 dimensions is $10^7 \times 768 = 7.68 \times 10^9$ multiply-adds per query, and $7.68 \times 10^9 \times 4$ bytes = **30.72 GB** of float32 data to stream through the CPU. Under a simple model where the scan is limited by a memory bandwidth of 100 GB/s, that is 30.72 GB divided by 100 GB per second, about 0.31 seconds for one query, before you serve a second user.

blocks.title: Brute-force latency grows linearly with collection size

scenes.caption: Simplified model: latency = N x d x 4 bytes / bandwidth. At 768 dimensions and 100 GB/s, 10 million vectors take about 307 ms per query, far over a 10 ms budget.
Ten times more bandwidth (1000 GB/s) only shifts the line down by 10x. The slope stays 1: double the data, double the time. Hardware cannot fix a linear scan.
Smaller vectors (128 dimensions) help by a constant factor too, but the line is still linear in N. We need an algorithm that looks at a tiny fraction of the vectors.

blocks.md: Classic exact indexes such as **k-d trees** speed this up only in low dimensions. A k-d tree (k-dimensional tree) splits the space in half on one coordinate, splits each half on the next coordinate, and so on; a search skips every box whose closest possible point is already farther than the best match found so far. The HNSW paper (Malkov and Yashunin, first posted in 2016, which introduced the index this course builds up to) puts it plainly: exact k-NN methods offer substantial speedups only for relatively low-dimensional data, because of the **curse of dimensionality**, Richard Bellman's name for the ways space behaves badly as the number of dimensions grows. One symptom is easy to measure: in high dimensions, the nearest and farthest points end up at almost the same distance, so pruning rules like "this whole region is too far away" rarely fire.

blocks.prompt: Draw 1000 random Gaussian points (every coordinate drawn from the bell-shaped standard normal distribution) and one random query. In 2 dimensions the farthest point is about 100 times farther than the nearest. What do you expect that ratio to be in 768 dimensions?
blocks.reveal: About **1.16**. We computed it (20 trials of 1000 points each): the ratio is 103 in 2-d (a noisy value, since the nearest point can land very close; another seed gave 127), 2.9 in 16-d, 1.44 in 128-d and 1.16 in 768-d. When every point is almost equally far, a tree cannot discard whole branches, so it degrades toward visiting everything. Why the ratio shrinks: a squared distance is a sum of d independent per-coordinate terms. Its average grows in proportion to d, but its spread grows only like the square root of d, so the spread relative to the average shrinks like 1 over the square root of d, and all distances bunch together.

blocks.title: Farthest over nearest distance, random Gaussian data

scenes.caption: Mean ratio of farthest to nearest distance from a random query to 1000 random Gaussian points (20 trials, computed with a script). In 2-d the contrast is huge.

Zoom on the high-dimensional cases: by 768-d the farthest point is only 16 percent farther than the nearest. Distance-based pruning has almost nothing to work with. (Real embeddings are less uniform than this, which is why ANN still works well on them.)

blocks.md: So practical systems give up on exactness. **Approximate nearest neighbor (ANN)** search allows a few mistakes in exchange for touching a tiny fraction of the data. Quality is measured by **recall@k**: the fraction of the true $k$ nearest neighbors (found by brute force) that the index returned. If the true top 5 is {3, 9, 14, 22, 40} and the index returns {3, 9, 14, 40, 51}, recall@5 is 4/5 = 0.8.

blocks.title: Measuring recall@5 against brute force

scenes.caption: Brute force gives the ground truth: the ids of the 5 vectors truly closest to the query, in order.
The ANN index returns 5 ids. Four of them (3, 9, 14, 40) are in the true top 5.
Id 22 was missed and id 51 slipped in. Recall@5 = 4/5 = 0.8. Order inside the top k does not matter for this metric.

blocks.md: ANN indexes trade a little recall for orders of magnitude fewer distance computations. Every ANN number you read (or report) should come as a pair: recall@k and speed, measured against exact brute-force results on the same queries.

Before graphs took over, the classic sublinear method was **locality-sensitive hashing (LSH)**: hash every vector so that nearby vectors are likely to land in the same bucket, then compare the query only with the vectors in its bucket. Charikar's random-hyperplane hash for cosine works like this: draw a random direction $r$ and record one bit, 1 if $r \cdot u \ge 0$ and 0 otherwise. Two vectors at angle $\theta$ get the same bit with probability $1 - \theta/\pi$, so close vectors agree on most bits. Concatenating $k$ bits makes a bucket key, which separates near from far sharply but also splits true neighbors apart, so LSH keeps $L$ independent tables and checks the query's bucket in each.

blocks.caption: A neighbor at angle theta shares all k bits of one key with probability (1 - theta/pi)^k; it is found if it collides in at least one of the L tables.

blocks.title: LSH: chance of finding a neighbor at a given angle

curves.label: found in at least one table

scenes.caption: One table with 16-bit keys: a neighbor at 10 degrees is found with probability 0.40, one at 30 degrees only 0.054. Long keys are selective but miss most true neighbors.
20 tables: the 30-degree neighbor is now found with probability 0.67, while a far vector at 60 degrees collides only 3 percent of the time. But every vector id is stored 20 times.
100 tables: 30 degrees reaches 0.996, but vectors at 45 degrees now collide 63 percent of the time and must be checked too. High recall costs many tables and many false candidates.

blocks.md: Those two costs are exactly what the documentation of Faiss (Meta's open-source vector search library) lists against classic LSH: it needs many hash functions (partitions) for acceptable results, which costs a lot of extra memory, and the hash functions are not adapted to the data. ANN-Benchmarks, which compares libraries on the same datasets, concluded that graph-based algorithms give by far the best performance on most of its datasets. The rest of this course follows that lead: graphs first, then the data-adapted partitions (IVF) and codes (PQ) that Faiss uses instead of random hashes.

Cosine similarity and inner product are not the same metric unless vectors are unit length; the prerequisite course's pooling lesson works through an example. An index fixes its metric at build time, so this matters here too. Faiss documents the standard fix: normalize vectors to length 1. Cosine is the inner product divided by both lengths, so when both lengths are 1 the two are equal.

blocks.question: Your collection grows from 1 million to 4 million vectors and you upgrade to a machine with 2x the memory bandwidth. Under the linear-scan model, what happens to brute-force latency?
options: It doubles: 4x the data over 2x the bandwidth
It stays the same, because the bandwidth doubled
It quadruples, because bandwidth does not affect latency
It halves, because more bandwidth beats more data
blocks.explain: Brute force reads every vector, so time scales with N divided by bandwidth: 4 / 2 = 2x slower. Hardware gives constant factors; the linear growth in N remains.

blocks.question: An index returns 10 results for a query; 7 of them are among the true 10 nearest neighbors. A colleague says recall@10 is 0.7, but because the 7 are ranked in a different order than the exact ones, the real recall is lower. Who is right?
options: The colleague: order mismatches reduce recall@10
Neither: recall needs the distances, not the ids
You: recall@10 counts overlap with the true top 10, so it is 0.7
The colleague: recall@10 is only defined for exact order
blocks.explain: Recall@k, as defined in the HNSW paper, is the number of true nearest neighbors found divided by k. It is a set overlap; ranking quality inside the top k is a separate metric.

blocks.question: With 16-bit keys, one LSH table finds a neighbor at 30 degrees only about 5 percent of the time. What is the standard fix, and what does it cost?
options: Use 32-bit keys, which raises the chance that close vectors collide
Switch to Euclidean distance, since LSH only struggles with cosine
Shrink the dataset, since collision probability falls as N grows
Add more independent tables, which multiplies the stored ids (memory) and the candidates to check
blocks.explain: Each table is an independent chance to collide, so L tables give 1 - (1 - p)^L. With 20 tables the 30-degree neighbor is found 67 percent of the time, at the price of 20 copies of every id. Longer keys make collisions rarer, not more likely, and the collision probability does not depend on N.

lessons.title: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters

blocks.md: A different idea: instead of partitioning space, connect each stored vector to a few of its near neighbors, forming a **proximity graph**. To search, start at some entry node and repeatedly hop to whichever neighbor is closer to the query. Each hop needs only a handful of distance computations, so if the path is short, the search is cheap.

This is the **Navigable Small World (NSW)** idea that HNSW builds on, an earlier single-layer graph method from the same lead author, Yury Malkov. A graph is *navigable* if greedy routing finds its target in a small (logarithmic or polylogarithmic) number of hops. Polylogarithmic means a power of $\log N$, such as $(\log N)^2$: still tiny next to $N$. The HNSW paper notes the ideal graph for this is the **Delaunay graph**. Give each stored point its Voronoi cell, the region of space closer to it than to any other stored point; the Delaunay graph links two points whenever their cells touch. In that graph greedy search always ends at the true nearest neighbor, but it cannot be built efficiently in high dimensions, so practical methods approximate it with near-neighbor links.

Here is a tiny hand-built graph of 8 points on a 2-d grid, with node A as the entry point. The query sits at grid position (5, 5). Each node's badge shows its Euclidean distance to the query, computed from grid coordinates. The true nearest neighbor is **H** at distance 1.41.

blocks.prompt: Greedy search starts at A and always moves to the neighbor closest to the query, stopping when no neighbor is closer than the current node. Trace it on the figure's first scene. Which node does it return?
blocks.reveal: It returns **F** (distance 2.0), not H (1.41). The path is A, C, D, F. At F, both neighbors (D at 2.83, E at 5.0) are farther from the query, so greedy stops. F is a **local minimum**: better than all its neighbors, but not the global best. The edge to H hangs off G, which greedy passed over because F looked better at D. The fix is to remember more than one node. A **beam search** keeps the best few nodes found so far, and the paper calls that number $ef$: it defines ef as the size of the dynamic list of nearest neighbors found so far, the beam width.

blocks.title: Greedy search gets stuck; a wider beam escapes

scenes.caption: Toy graph (hand-built, 8 nodes). Badges show each node's distance to the query. Entry point A is far away (7.07). The true nearest neighbor is H (1.41).
Greedy, step 1: at A, compute distances to neighbors B (5.0) and C (4.47). C is closest to the query, so hop to C.
Step 2: C's new neighbors are D (2.83) and E (5.0). Hop to D. Each hop costs only one distance per new neighbor.
Step 3: at D, neighbors F (2.0) and G (3.0) are new. F is closest, so greedy hops to F and forgets G.
Step 4: F's neighbors D (2.83) and E (5.0) are both farther than F (2.0). Greedy stops and returns F. It never saw H: a local minimum after 7 distance evaluations.
Beam search with ef = 3 keeps the 3 best nodes found so far, not just 1. After expanding D the list is F (2.0), D (2.83), G (3.0), so G stays in play.
Expanding F adds nothing new, so the search expands G next and discovers H (1.41). The final list is H, F, D: the true nearest neighbor is found, at the cost of one more distance (8 in total).

blocks.md: The fix shown in the last two scenes is the search procedure HNSW actually uses (Algorithm 2, SEARCH-LAYER, in the paper). It keeps two sets: **C**, the candidates still to expand, ordered nearest first, and **W**, the best $ef$ nodes found so far. It repeatedly expands the nearest candidate and stops when the nearest remaining candidate is farther than the worst member of W, because nothing reachable through it can improve W.

blocks.title: SEARCH-LAYER on the toy graph with ef = 3

scenes.caption: Start at entry point A (7.07). Both lists hold just A.
Expand A. W has room (fewer than 3), so B (5.0) and C (4.47) are added to both lists.
Expand C. D (2.83) beats the worst of W and enters; A is evicted. E (5.0) is not strictly better than B (5.0), so it is skipped.
Expand D. F (2.0) and G (3.0) both beat the worst of W, pushing out B and C. With ef = 1, G would have been dropped here.
Expand F. Its neighbors D and E were already visited, so nothing changes.
Expand G. H (1.41) is new and better than the worst member (G 3.0), so H enters and G leaves W.
Expand H: no new neighbors. Next candidate is B at 5.0, farther than W's worst (D 2.83), so the loop breaks and returns W.

blocks.md: $ef$ is the size of the result list W. A larger $ef$ explores more of the graph, escapes more local minima and raises recall, at the cost of more distance computations. To return $k$ results you need $ef \ge k$; hnswlib (the reference C++ and Python implementation of HNSW) documents that ef cannot be set lower than k.

Greedy graph search has no guarantee of exactness on a real (non-Delaunay) graph. Even a large $ef$ can miss a neighbor if the graph has no path that improves toward it. Recall comes from how well the graph is built, which is the subject of the next two lessons.

blocks.question: In SEARCH-LAYER, why is it safe to stop when the nearest remaining candidate is farther than the worst element of W?
options: Because the graph is guaranteed to be a Delaunay graph
Because every remaining candidate is farther than all ef results, and the search assumes their neighbors are unlikely to be closer; it is a heuristic stop, not a proof
Because all ef results have already been found exactly
Because distances in high dimensions are all equal
blocks.explain: Candidates farther than W's worst cannot enter W, and the search assumes their neighbors are unlikely to be better. That is the approximation: on a well-built graph it rarely loses true neighbors, but it is not an exactness guarantee.

blocks.question: On the toy graph, greedy search (ef = 1) returned F instead of H. Which change would most directly let it find H?
options: Start from F instead of A
Use cosine distance instead of Euclidean
Remove the edge between D and F
Raise ef so G is kept in the result list
blocks.explain: With ef = 3, G (3.0) survives in W after D is expanded, and expanding G reveals H. Changing the start node or edges is not something you control per query; ef is the query-time knob.

lessons.title: HNSW layers: a skip list made of graphs

blocks.md: A flat NSW graph has a scaling problem. The HNSW paper explains that greedy routing in NSW has polylogarithmic complexity: the number of hops grows with $\log N$, and the number of links checked at each hub (a node with many links) also grows with $\log N$, so the total work grows like $(\log N)^2$. Search starts with many short hops before it reaches the region of the query.

HNSW fixes this the way a **skip list** speeds up a sorted linked list. A skip list keeps the full list at the bottom, plus sparser "express" lists above it that skip many elements per step. Each element is copied up to the next express list with probability $p$ (often 1/2), so each list holds about $p$ times as many elements as the one below. HNSW does the same with graphs: layer 0 holds every vector; each higher layer holds a random, exponentially smaller subset, so its links span longer distances. Search starts at the top, takes a few long hops, then drops a layer and refines.

Each vector's top layer, its **level** $\ell$, is chosen at random when it is inserted (line 4 of the paper's Algorithm 1). The recipe uses $M$, the number of links each new node creates per layer (lesson 4 covers how they are chosen), and a constant $m_L$ the paper calls the normalization factor for level generation:

blocks.caption: In words: draw u uniformly between 0 and 1, take minus its natural log, multiply by m_L and round down. A vector with level l is present in layers 0 through l. The paper recommends m_L = 1/ln M, and hnswlib sets mult_ = 1 / log(M).

blocks.md: With $m_L = 1/\ln M$, the probability that a vector reaches layer $\ell$ or higher is $M^{-\ell}$. Here is why. The level is at least $\ell$ exactly when $-\ln(u) \cdot m_L \ge \ell$, that is when $-\ln u \ge \ell \ln M$, that is when $u \le e^{-\ell \ln M} = M^{-\ell}$. A uniform $u$ falls below $M^{-\ell}$ with probability exactly $M^{-\ell}$. With $M = 4$, a quarter of vectors reach layer 1 and a sixteenth reach layer 2. The paper notes this matches a skip list with $p = 1/M$, which gives each layer about $1/M$ as many nodes as the one below. So the same $M$ sets both the fan-out and the layer shrink rate.

blocks.title: Sampling levels for 10 inserts with M = 4

scenes.caption: Ten uniform random draws (seeded script). With M = 4, mL = 1/ln 4 = 0.721.
Transform each draw: -ln(u) x 0.721. Small u gives a large value; this produces an exponential distribution.
Floor gives the level. Six of ten land on layer 0 only. Four reach layer 1 or higher (expected 10 x 1/4 = 2.5).

Element 6 drew level 3, the highest so far, so it becomes the entry point: every search starts at its top layer. If a later insert draws a higher level, it takes over (lines 18 and 19 of Algorithm 1).

blocks.title: Expected nodes per layer: 1 million vectors, M = 16

scenes.caption: Layer 0 holds all 1,000,000 vectors. On a linear axis everything else is invisible: the upper layers are tiny.
Without layer 0: N x 16^-l gives 62,500 nodes on layer 1, 3,906 on layer 2, 244 on layer 3, 15 on layer 4 and about 1 on layer 5. The top layer is near log base 16 of 10^6 = 4.98.

blocks.md: Search (Algorithm 5 in the paper) uses this structure in two phases. On every layer above 0 it runs SEARCH-LAYER with $ef = 1$, a plain greedy descent, and uses the node it ends on as the entry point for the next layer down. On layer 0 it runs SEARCH-LAYER with the user's $ef$ and returns the best $k$ of the result list.

blocks.title: Descending the layers on the toy graph

scenes.caption: Simplified: we assign levels by hand (A and G at level 2, H at level 1, the rest at 0). Layer 2 holds only A and G, linked by one long edge. Search starts at the entry point A.
Greedy on layer 2: G (3.0) is closer than A (7.07), so hop to G. G has no closer neighbor here, so G becomes the entry point for layer 1. One long hop crossed most of the space.
Layer 1 holds A, G and H. From G, neighbor H (1.41) is closer, so hop to H. H has no closer neighbor on this layer.
Layer 0 has every node. Starting from H, even plain greedy (ef = 1) cannot improve: H is the answer. Flat greedy from A ended at F; starting near the target avoids that local minimum.

blocks.md: The hierarchy also has a modest memory cost. Each node stores up to $M_{max0}$ links on layer 0 and up to $M_{max}$ on each upper layer it belongs to. The paper approximates the average number of upper layers per node by $m_L$ (the exact value with the floor is the sum of the chances of reaching layers 1, 2, 3 and so on, $1/M + 1/M^2 + \dots = 1/(M-1)$, about 0.067 for $M = 16$, against $m_L \approx 0.361$; that overestimates the upper-layer term about fivefold, but layer 0 dominates, so the total below is about 151 bytes instead of about 132), and gives the average graph memory per vector as:

blocks.caption: In words: 32 layer-0 links plus 0.361 times 16, about 5.8 upper-layer links, times 4 bytes per link id, is about 151 bytes. Here M = 16, M_max = M and M_max0 = 2M. The paper reports 60 to 450 bytes per object for M from 6 to 48.

blocks.md: Compare that with the vector itself: 768 float32 dimensions are 3,072 bytes, so the graph adds about 5 percent. For HNSW the dominant memory cost is usually the raw vectors, which must stay in RAM because every hop computes exact distances against them.

blocks.question: With M = 16 and the recommended m_L, roughly what fraction of vectors appear on layer 2 or above?
options: 1/16, about 6 percent
1/32, about 3 percent
1/256, about 0.4 percent
1/2, because each layer halves
blocks.explain: P(level at least l) = M^-l, so layer 2 or above has probability 16^-2 = 1/256. Layer 1 or above is 1/16. The shrink factor per layer is M, not 2.

blocks.question: A teammate sets m_L very high (for example 5) so the hierarchy is taller. What does the HNSW paper say happens when m_L is too large?
options: Recall drops to zero because layer 0 becomes empty
Memory shrinks because fewer links are stored
Neighbors overlap more across layers, so extra layers add little and search gets slower
Nothing changes; m_L only affects build time
blocks.explain: The paper explains that larger m_L means more overlap between layers (more nodes repeated on many layers), which hurts performance, while too small m_L increases the number of hops on each layer. That tradeoff is why it picks m_L = 1/ln M, matching a skip list with p = 1/M.

lessons.title: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic

blocks.md: HNSW is built by inserting vectors one at a time (Algorithm 1 in the paper). Inserting vector $q$ looks a lot like searching for it:

1. Draw $q$'s level $\ell$ with the formula from the last lesson.
2. From the entry point, descend greedily ($ef = 1$) through the layers above $\ell$.
3. On each layer from $\min(L, \ell)$ down to 0, where $L$ is the index's current top layer, run SEARCH-LAYER with $ef = ef_{construction}$ (the beam width used while building, covered below) to collect candidates, pick $M$ of them as $q$'s neighbors, and add links in **both** directions.
4. If a neighbor now has more than $M_{max}$ links ($M_{max0}$ on layer 0), shrink its list with the same selection rule.
5. If $\ell$ is above the current top layer, $q$ becomes the new entry point.

Step 3 hides the key design choice: *which* $M$ candidates become neighbors. The simple rule (Algorithm 3) takes the $M$ closest. The paper's **heuristic** (Algorithm 4) walks candidates from nearest to farthest and keeps candidate $e$ only if $e$ is closer to $q$ than to every neighbor already kept. A candidate that is closer to a kept neighbor is skipped, because $q$ can already reach it through that neighbor. The kept links point in different directions, which is why it is often called a diversity heuristic.

blocks.tex: \text{keep } e \iff \operatorname{dist}(e, q) < \operatorname{dist}(e, r) \ \text{ for every already-kept } r \in R
blocks.caption: Paper Algorithm 4, line 11. hnswlib's getNeighborsByHeuristic2 implements the same test.

blocks.prompt: New node q has two clusters of candidates: e1, e2, e3 close by on its left (distances 1.0, 2.0, 1.41) and e4, e5 farther away on its right (3.0, 3.16). With M = 2, which two neighbors does each rule pick?
blocks.reveal: The **simple rule** picks e1 and e3, the two closest, both in the left cluster. The **heuristic** keeps e1, rejects e3 (it is 1.0 from e1 but 1.41 from q) and e2 (1.0 from e1, 2.0 from q), then keeps e4 (4.0 from e1, only 3.0 from q). Result: e1 and e4, one link into each cluster.

blocks.title: Neighbor selection: simple rule vs heuristic (M = 2)

scenes.caption: Candidates found by SEARCH-LAYER for new node q, with distances to q (grid coordinates, computed). The left cluster is close; the right cluster is reachable only through q's links.
Simple rule: keep the 2 closest, e1 (1.0) and e3 (1.41). Both are in the left cluster. Nothing links q toward the right cluster.
Heuristic, nearest first: e1 (1.0) is kept automatically because R is empty.
e3: distance to e1 is 1.0, less than its distance to q (1.41). q can already reach e3 through e1, so e3 is skipped. e2 fails the same way (1.0 to e1 vs 2.0 to q).
e4: distance to e1 is 4.0, more than its 3.0 to q, so it is kept. R is now full (M = 2). The heuristic chose one link per direction, a bridge between clusters.

blocks.md: Why does that matter? On clustered data, the simple rule links each new node only into its own cluster, and clusters can end up disconnected: no greedy path leads from one to another. The paper says the heuristic helps most on clustered data and makes little difference on uniform, very high-dimensional data. We checked this with the compact pure-Python implementation below. It builds layer 0 only (every node, no hierarchy, node 0 as a fixed entry point), which is all you need to compare the two selection rules; adding the upper layers is the exercise at the end of this lesson.

blocks.code:
import heapq
import numpy as np

class Layer0:  # HNSW layer 0 only; node 0 is the entry point
    def __init__(self, x, M=8, ef_construction=64, heuristic=True):
        self.x, self.M, self.Mmax0 = x, M, 2 * M
        self.efc, self.heuristic = ef_construction, heuristic
        self.links = [[] for _ in range(len(x))]
        self.ndist = 0                    # distance counter

    def d(self, q, ids):                  # squared L2 to many ids
        self.ndist += len(ids)
        return ((self.x[ids] - q) ** 2).sum(axis=1)

    def search(self, q, ef, ep=0):        # SEARCH-LAYER (Alg. 2)
        d0 = self.d(q, [ep])[0]
        seen, C, W = {ep}, [(d0, ep)], [(-d0, ep)]
        while C:
            dc, c = heapq.heappop(C)      # nearest candidate
            if dc > -W[0][0]:             # worse than worst in W
                break
            new = [e for e in self.links[c] if e not in seen]
            seen.update(new)
            for de, e in zip(self.d(q, new) if new else [], new):
                if len(W) < ef or de < -W[0][0]:
                    heapq.heappush(C, (de, e))
                    heapq.heappush(W, (-de, e))
                    if len(W) > ef:
                        heapq.heappop(W)  # drop the furthest
        return sorted((-nd, e) for nd, e in W)
blocks.caption: Part 1: the graph and SEARCH-LAYER with two heaps (C holds candidates nearest first; W holds the best ef, worst on top). Same logic as the trace in lesson 2.

Part 2: neighbor selection (simple or heuristic), insertion with reverse links and pruning, then a build and a query. This code produced the numbers below: the bars with M = 8 and ef_construction = 64 on synthetic data, the SIFT10K check with the settings shown.

scenes.caption: Setup: 20,000 vectors in 16-d, M = 8, M_max0 = 16, ef_construction = 64, 200 queries, recall@10 vs brute force. Uniform = one Gaussian; clustered = 50 Gaussian clusters whose centers spread 4 times wider than each cluster. At ef = 64:

Doubling ef to 128 helps the uniform graphs, but the simple rule on clustered data barely moves (78.2 percent, against 99.9 with the heuristic): the missing neighbors sit in clusters that greedy search cannot reach. More search effort cannot fix missing links.

blocks.md: Is a 55-line toy trustworthy? We compared it with hnswlib on **SIFT10K**, a public benchmark from the TEXMEX corpus: 10,000 SIFT descriptors (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform: 128 numbers summarizing the image gradients around one keypoint), 100 queries and published ground truth. With M = 16 and ef_construction = 200, our layer-0 graph reached recall@10 of 92.2, 98.2 and 99.6 percent at ef = 10, 20 and 40; hnswlib, with its full hierarchy, reached 93.4, 98.2 and 99.6. At 10,000 vectors the upper layers barely matter; lesson 3 showed why they pay off as N grows.

Exercise: add the hierarchy. Draw each node's level with $\lfloor -\ln(u) \cdot m_L \rfloor$, keep one links list per layer, descend with `search(q, ef=1)` on every layer above the node's level, then insert on each layer from the lower of its level and the current top layer down to 0 with $M_{max} = M$ above layer 0. The node with the highest level becomes the entry point.

The construction parameters, as documented in the paper and hnswlib:

- **M**: links created per new node per layer. The paper suggests 5 to 48; hnswlib says 12 to 48 suits most uses, with higher M for high intrinsic dimensionality (the number of independent directions the data really varies along, which can be far below the stored dimension d) or high recall. Memory grows linearly in M.
- **M_max0 = 2M** on layer 0. The paper found $M_{max0} = M$ causes a strong penalty at high recall, and values above 2M waste memory without speedup.
- **ef_construction**: the beam width while inserting. It should be large enough that construction-time search reaches recall near 1 (the paper says 0.95 is enough for most uses); beyond that, raising it only slows the build.
hnswlib's check for a good ef_construction: build the index, set ef = ef_construction, and measure recall for an M-nearest-neighbor search. If recall is below 0.9, there is room to improve the graph.

Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; the last lesson shows how libraries and disk-based systems handle them.

blocks.question: You build HNSW over product embeddings grouped into tight categories, using the simple closest-M rule. Recall plateaus near 80 percent no matter how high you set ef. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: ef is still too low; raise it to 10,000
M_max0 is too large; set it equal to M
The level formula is wrong; set m_L to 0
The categories are disconnected in the graph; use the diversity heuristic when selecting neighbors
blocks.explain: A plateau that ef cannot lift means the graph lacks paths, not search effort. The heuristic keeps links that point in diverse directions, including bridges between clusters, which is exactly the case the paper's Figure 2 illustrates.

blocks.question: Which change increases index build time but leaves query-time cost per ef roughly the same?
options: Raising ef at query time
Raising ef_construction
Raising M
Raising the dimension d
blocks.explain: ef_construction only controls the beam width during inserts. M also raises query cost because every expanded node has more neighbors to score; d makes every distance more expensive; ef is the query knob itself.

lessons.title: IVF: clustering the space, nlist and nprobe

blocks.md: HNSW links vectors to each other. The second big family of ANN indexes partitions them instead, like a library that shelves books by topic: to find a book you walk to the one or two most promising shelves and ignore the rest. Faiss calls this an **inverted file (IVF)**. Each vector is filed under its nearest **centroid**, a representative point for one region of space. Each centroid keeps a list of its vectors, like a word's list of documents in a search engine's inverted index, hence the name. A query is compared with the centroids first, then only with the vectors filed under the closest few.

The centroids come from **k-means** clustering, run once at training time. Pick $k$ starting centroids (here, three of the data points), then repeat two steps until nothing changes: **assign** every vector to its nearest centroid, and **update** every centroid to the mean of the vectors assigned to it. Faiss calls the number of centroids `nlist` (the number of inverted lists) and the number of lists a query scans `nprobe`. The figure runs k-means on 12 points in 2-d with nlist = 3, then answers one query.

blocks.prompt: Watch the last three scenes. The query sits at (3, 3), between the bottom cell and the right cell. With nprobe = 1 the index scans only the cell whose centroid is closest. Does it find the true nearest neighbor?
blocks.reveal: No. The closest centroid is c2 at (3, 5.25), distance 2.25; c3 at (4.75, 1.0) is 2.66 away. Scanning c2's cell returns p12 at distance 2.0, but the true nearest neighbor is **p8** at 1.41, filed in c3's cell. That is IVF's failure mode: the neighbor sits just across a cell boundary. With nprobe = 2, c3's cell is scanned too and p8 is found. Cost: 3 centroid distances plus 4 vectors = 7 with nprobe = 1, and 3 + 8 = 11 with nprobe = 2, against 12 for brute force.

blocks.title: k-means builds the cells, then a query probes them

scenes.caption: Twelve points on a grid (hand-placed). k-means starts from three of the points as centroids: p1, p4 and p5.
Assign: every point joins its nearest starting centroid. p4 is a starting centroid itself, so it pulls the whole bottom group (p9 to p12) into cell 2.
Update: each centroid moves to the mean of its cell. Centroids are drawn at the nearest free grid cell; the labels give their exact coordinates.
Assign again. p4 at (1, 2) is now 1.80 from c1 but 3.05 from c2, so it switches to cell 1. No other point changes cell.
Update: c1 moves to (0.5, 0.75) and c2 to (3.0, 5.25). One more assign step changes nothing, so k-means has converged: three cells of four points each.
A query arrives at (3, 3). IVF search step 1: compute its distance to the three centroids: 3.36 to c1, 2.25 to c2, 2.66 to c3.
nprobe = 1: scan only c2's list (p9 to p12). The best is p12 at 2.0, after 3 + 4 = 7 distances. But the true nearest neighbor, p8 at 1.41, sits in c3's cell, which was never opened.
nprobe = 2: also scan c3's list (p5 to p8). p8 at 1.41 wins, after 3 + 8 = 11 distances against 12 for brute force. On 12 points the saving is tiny; on millions it is the whole point.

blocks.md: How many cells? The Faiss library paper (Douze and others, 2024) gives the cost model. Assume the centroids are scanned exhaustively, the lists hold full vectors, and all lists have the same size $N/n_{list}$. A query computes $n_{list}$ centroid distances, then scans $n_{probe}$ lists:

blocks.tex: N_{\text{dist}} = n_{list} + n_{probe} \cdot \frac{N}{n_{list}}, \qquad \frac{dN_{\text{dist}}}{dn_{list}} = 1 - \frac{n_{probe} N}{n_{list}^2} = 0 \quad \text{at} \quad n_{list} = \sqrt{n_{probe} N}
blocks.caption: Equation 18 of the Faiss library paper, and its minimum: setting the derivative to zero gives nlist = sqrt(nprobe x N), where both terms are equal. That is the origin of the usual rule that nlist should grow like the square root of N.

blocks.title: IVF cost model: distances per query vs nlist

curves.label: IVF: nlist + nprobe x N / nlist

scenes.caption: N = 1 million, nprobe = 1: the minimum, 2,000 distances (0.2 percent of brute force), is at nlist = 1,000. Too few lists and each one is huge; too many and scanning the centroids dominates.
nprobe = 16, for higher recall, moves the optimum to 4,000 lists and 8,000 distances, still under 1 percent of brute force.
At 100 million vectors the optimum is 40,000 lists and 80,000 distances. Brute force grew 100x from 1 million; the IVF optimum grew 10x, like the square root of N.

blocks.md: The paper calls this a rough approximation: nprobe has to grow with nlist to keep the same accuracy, the lists are not equal in size, and large indexes often find the nearest centroids with an HNSW index instead of scanning all of them. That is why the practical guidelines sit above the bare optimum. Faiss's guide suggests nlist between $4\sqrt{N}$ and $16\sqrt{N}$ below 1 million vectors. pgvector suggests lists = rows/1000 up to 1 million rows and sqrt(rows) beyond, with probes = sqrt(lists) as a starting point.

blocks.title: IVF on SIFT10K: recall and work vs nprobe (nlist = 100)

scenes.caption: Faiss IndexIVFFlat on SIFT10K (10,000 vectors, 128-d), nlist = 100 trained with k-means on the 25,000 separate learning vectors, 100 queries. Recall@10: one probe finds only half of the true neighbors.
Distances per query (100 centroids plus the scanned vectors) as a percent of the 10,000 brute-force distances: 2.2, 3.3, 5.3, 9.2, 17.0 and 31.9. Each doubling of nprobe roughly doubles the scan.

blocks.md: The best nlist depends on the recall you need. In the same run, getting to about 97 to 99 percent took nprobe = 4 with nlist = 25 (96.7 percent recall, 17.3 percent of brute-force distances), nprobe = 16 with nlist = 100 (98.7 percent, 17.0) and nprobe = 32 with nlist = 400 (97.6 percent, 12.7). For nprobe = 16 and N = 10,000 the model's optimum is nlist = 400, and it did need the fewest distances. Yet all three ran at about the same speed on one thread of an Apple Silicon CPU: 80,000, 78,000 and 77,000 queries per second in this run, and 66,000, 63,000 and 68,000 in a rerun, so their order is noise. Distance counts are a model of cost, not a measurement: time the real thing, more than once.

IVF has a **training** step, which HNSW does not: k-means needs a sample that looks like the data. Faiss asks for between 30 x nlist and 256 x nlist training vectors (we used 25,000 for nlist = 100, 250 per centroid). Cells also come out unequal: our 100 lists held between 5 and 300 vectors, against a mean of 100. The Faiss paper measures this with the **imbalance factor**, the mean of the squared list sizes divided by the square of the mean size (1 when all are equal; 1.20 for our lists), and the expected number of distance computations is multiplied by it.

Training also freezes the centroids. If the data drifts, new vectors pile into whichever old cells are nearest. We simulated this by training on only the quarter of the learning set with the smallest first coordinate, then adding all 10,000 vectors: the five largest lists grew from 1,139 to 2,144 vectors in total, and each query at nprobe = 4 scanned 756 vectors instead of 432 (recall rose a little, 86.1 against 83.0 percent, only because more was scanned). pgvector's README gives the same advice from the other side: create an IVFFlat index after the table has data, and if a query returns fewer rows after the index is added, the index was likely created with too little data for its number of lists. When the distribution moves, retrain and rebuild.

blocks.code:
import faiss

d, nlist = 128, 100
quantizer = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d)     # exact search over the centroids
index = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(quantizer, d, nlist)
index.train(xt)                      # k-means on 25,000 learning vectors
index.add(xb)                        # file each vector under its centroid

for nprobe in (1, 4, 16):
    index.nprobe = nprobe
    D, I = index.search(xq, 10)
    print(nprobe, recall_at_10(I, gt))
# 1 0.505
# 4 0.83
# 16 0.987
blocks.caption: The SIFT10K run behind the bars (faiss-cpu 1.16, one thread). recall_at_10 compares each result list with the dataset's published ground truth.

blocks.md: IVF costs about nlist + nprobe x N/nlist distances per query. nprobe is the query-time knob, like ef in HNSW: each extra probe opens one more cell and catches neighbors that sit across a boundary, at a cost roughly proportional to the extra vectors scanned.

An IVF index is only as good as its training sample. Train on too few vectors, or on data that no longer looks like what you store, and the lists become unbalanced: some probes scan huge lists and every query pays for them.

blocks.question: Your IVF index (nlist = 4,096) gives 70 percent recall@10 at nprobe = 1 and you need 95. Memory is fine. What is the right first move, and what does it cost?
options: Raise nlist to 65,536 and keep nprobe = 1, since smaller cells make each probe more precise
Retrain k-means with more iterations, since recall at nprobe = 1 is set by centroid precision
Raise nprobe and re-measure; each extra probe scans roughly another N/nlist vectors, so cost grows about linearly with nprobe
Lower nlist to 64 and keep nprobe = 1, which keeps the cost the same
blocks.explain: Misses at nprobe = 1 are neighbors filed in nearby cells, and probing more cells is the direct fix. In our SIFT10K run recall went from 50.5 to 83.0 to 98.7 percent as nprobe went 1, 4, 16, while scanned vectors grew from 122 to 432 to 1,599 per query. More lists at the same nprobe scan less and miss more; far fewer lists make every probe much more expensive.

blocks.question: You build an IVF index with nlist = 4,096. Following Faiss's guideline, how large should the k-means training sample be?
options: Between about 123,000 and 1 million vectors (30 to 256 per centroid)
At least 4,096 vectors, one per centroid
Exactly 64 vectors, the square root of 4,096
None: the inverted lists are built without training
blocks.explain: Faiss asks for between 30 x K and 256 x K training vectors for K centroids: 30 x 4,096 = 122,880 and 256 x 4,096 = 1,048,576. One vector per centroid gives k-means nothing to average, and IVF, unlike HNSW, cannot be built without training.

lessons.title: Product quantization by hand: codebooks, lookup tables, re-ranking

blocks.md: IVF cuts how many vectors a query touches, but every stored vector still costs 4 bytes per dimension. To shrink the vectors themselves, replace each one with a short code, the way a paint-by-numbers kit replaces every exact color with the number of the nearest paint in a small palette. That is **quantization**: replace a value with the nearest entry of a fixed set, the **codebook**, and store only the entry's index. A k-means codebook of 256 centroids turns any vector into a 1-byte code.

One codebook for whole vectors does not scale: with 1 byte, all 128 dimensions of a SIFT vector must be approximated by one of only 256 points. The Faiss library paper notes that a plain k-means quantizer is impractical beyond roughly 3-byte codes (16 million centroids). **Product quantization (PQ)** splits each vector into $m$ sub-vectors and gives each slice its own small codebook of $k^*$ entries, learned with k-means on that slice of the training data. A code is $m$ small indices, and together they can name $(k^*)^m$ different reconstructions: $2^{64}$ for 8 one-byte indices. (This $m$ is unrelated to HNSW's $M$.)

blocks.tex: c_j(x) = \arg\min_{i} \lVert x^{(j)} - C_j[i] \rVert^2, \quad j = 1, \dots, m, \qquad \text{code size} = m \log_2 k^* \text{ bits}
blocks.caption: Each slice of x is encoded on its own, to the index of its nearest entry in that slice's codebook. With 256 entries per codebook each index is one byte, so a vector costs m bytes.

blocks.md: A toy you can check by hand: 8-d vectors, $m = 4$ slices of 2 dimensions, and $k^* = 4$ entries per codebook, so each index takes 2 bits and a whole code takes 8 bits. We trained the four codebooks with k-means on 200 random Gaussian vectors and rounded them to one decimal; every number below was computed from these rounded codebooks with a script.

blocks.title: Four codebooks for 8-d vectors (m = 4, 4 entries each)

scenes.caption: Each pair of columns is one codebook for one 2-d slice (s1 to s4); each row is one entry. These 32 numbers describe 4 x 4 x 4 x 4 = 256 possible reconstructions.
Encode x1 = (-0.9, 0.9 | -1.6, -0.2 | 0.8, 0.0 | 0.8, -0.6). Each slice picks its nearest entry: 0, 0, 0 and 3. The code (0, 0, 0, 3) takes 8 bits instead of 32 bytes.
x2 = (0.4, 0.9 | 2.2, 0.7 | 1.4, 0.0 | 0.1, 1.6) encodes to (1, 1, 0, 2). Its slice s2 = (2.2, 0.7) lies outside every entry of that codebook; the nearest, (0.6, 1.0), is 1.63 away.

blocks.md: To search, the query stays exact. Split $q$ the same way and compute, once per query, the squared distance from each query slice to every entry of that slice's codebook: an $m \times k^*$ table. The distance to any stored vector is then estimated by looking up one table cell per slice and adding. This is the **asymmetric distance computation (ADC)**, asymmetric because only the database side is compressed. The GPU Faiss paper (Johnson, Douze and Jégou) counts the saving: with 256-entry codebooks the tables cost $256 \times d$ multiply-adds, after which each of the $n$ vectors costs $m$ lookup-adds instead of $d$ multiply-adds.

blocks.caption: The table T is built once per query. Every stored vector then costs m lookups and additions, independent of the dimension d.

blocks.title: The per-query distance table, and two estimates

scenes.caption: Query q = (0.6, 1.4 | 0.7, 2.1 | 2.4, -0.8 | 1.9, 0.5), not quantized. Each cell is the squared distance from one query slice to one codebook entry: 16 numbers, computed once per query.
x1, code (0, 0, 0, 3): 1.93 + 11.25 + 2.34 + 2.96 = 18.48. The exact squared distance is 18.70, so the estimate is off by about 1 percent.
x2, code (1, 1, 0, 2): 0.40 + 1.22 + 2.34 + 0.85 = 4.81, but the exact squared distance is 10.59. The ranking is still right (x2 is closer than x1), yet the estimate is less than half the truth.

blocks.prompt: Why is x2's estimate (4.81 against 10.59) so far off, while x1's (18.48 against 18.70) is nearly exact?
blocks.reveal: ADC measures the distance from q to x2's **reconstruction**, the concatenated codebook entries (0.8, 0.8 | 0.6, 1.0 | 0.9, -0.5 | 1.0, 0.7), not to x2 itself. x2's second slice (2.2, 0.7) is 1.63 from its nearest entry, and its total squared reconstruction error is 4.94, against 1.62 for x1. Small codebooks cannot represent outliers, and that error lands directly in the estimate. Real codebooks have 256 entries per slice, which shrinks the error but never removes it.

blocks.md: You could also quantize the query and add up distances between codebook entries, the **symmetric** version (SDC). The Faiss library paper notes that most Faiss indexes use ADC because it is more accurate: no accuracy is lost on the query. In our toy the query's own code is (1, 1, 0, 2), identical to x2's, so SDC would put x2 at distance 0. The product-quantization course works through SDC, ADC and their errors in detail.

blocks.title: PQ on SIFT10K: recall@10 before and after re-ranking

scenes.caption: Faiss IndexPQ on SIFT10K (256-entry codebooks trained on the learning set), exhaustive ADC scan, recall@10. The raw vectors take 512 bytes; 8 to 32-byte codes lose many true neighbors.
Re-ranking: take the top 40 by PQ distance (k_factor = 4), recompute exact distances with the full vectors, keep the best 10. Recall jumps to 89.4, 99.1 and 99.9 percent.
A shortlist of 100 (k_factor = 10) lifts even 8-byte codes to 97.7 percent. The codes only need to put the true neighbors into the shortlist, not in the right order.

blocks.md: That last caption is the idea to keep. The Faiss library paper describes **refinement** as querying a fast, inaccurate index for a shortlist and then computing more accurate distances only for the shortlist; for the first stage, the metric that matters is recall at the shortlist size. The estimates the index returns are also skewed: for each query's top 100, the PQ8 estimate averaged 11 percent below the true squared distance (PQ16: 4 percent, PQ32: 1 percent), partly because the scan keeps exactly the vectors whose estimates came out low. Never apply a distance threshold to raw PQ distances; re-rank first.

**IVFPQ** combines this lesson with the last one: IVF picks the cells and PQ compresses the vectors inside them. Faiss encodes the **residual**, the vector minus its cell's centroid, rather than the vector itself (the `by_residual` flag, on by default); the Faiss paper says this is generally more accurate because residuals are smaller than the vectors, with the largest benefit for short codes. On SIFT10K with nlist = 100, 16-byte codes and nprobe = 16 we measured 72.2 percent recall@10 with residuals and 71.5 without, a small gain at this size. Storage is $m$ bytes of code plus an 8-byte id: for 1 billion 768-d vectors with $m = 96$, that is 104 bytes per vector, about 104 GB, against 3.07 TB of float32.

Three refinements, covered in later courses. **OPQ** (optimized product quantization) applies a learned linear transform before PQ so that the vectors are easier to compress (Faiss's guide). **ScaNN's anisotropic quantization** (Guo and others, 2019) trains codebooks for inner-product search with a loss that penalizes the part of the error parallel to the data point more than the orthogonal part. **RaBitQ** (Gao and Long, 2024) quantizes D-dimensional vectors into D-bit strings with a theoretical error bound; Faiss lists it at d/8 + 8 bytes per vector. See the product-quantization and RaBitQ courses.

blocks.code:
import faiss

pq = faiss.IndexPQ(128, 16, 8)     # m = 16 sub-vectors, 8 bits (256 entries) each
index = faiss.IndexRefineFlat(pq)  # also keeps the float vectors for re-ranking
index.train(xt)
index.add(xb)

D, I = pq.search(xq, 10)           # PQ alone:            recall@10 = 0.721
index.k_factor = 4                 # shortlist of 40, then exact distances
D, I = index.search(xq, 10)        # PQ plus re-ranking:  recall@10 = 0.991
blocks.caption: The SIFT10K run behind the bars (faiss-cpu 1.16). In this form IndexRefineFlat stores the float vectors in RAM next to the codes, so it buys accuracy, not memory; DiskANN in the last lesson keeps them on SSD instead.

blocks.md: PQ stores m bytes per vector and estimates each distance with m table lookups. The estimates are good enough to build a shortlist, not to set the final order: keep the full vectors somewhere and re-rank the top few dozen.

blocks.question: With 16-byte PQ codes on SIFT10K, recall@10 is 72 percent; re-ranking the top 40 with exact distances raises it to 99 percent. What does the re-ranking step need?
options: Nothing extra: exact distances can be recovered from the PQ codes
Random access to the full-precision vectors of the 40 candidates, and 40 exact distance computations per query
A second codebook with 256 more entries per slice
Codebooks retrained on the query vectors
blocks.explain: A code only names a reconstruction, so the exact distance cannot be recovered from it. Re-ranking reads the original vectors of the shortlist (from RAM or SSD) and computes exact distances for those 40 only. That is why systems that compress for memory still keep the full vectors somewhere cheaper.

blocks.question: What makes the per-query table the source of PQ's speed?
options: It stores every vector's exact distance, computed at build time
It lets the scan skip every vector whose code differs from the query's code
It replaces k-means, so no training is needed
It is computed once per query (m x 256 entries), after which each stored vector costs m lookups and additions instead of d multiply-adds
blocks.explain: The table depends only on the query and the codebooks, so its cost is paid once. Scanning n vectors then costs n x m lookup-adds: 16 for a 16-byte code, against 128 multiply-adds for a 128-d float vector. The table cannot be built at index time because it depends on the query.

lessons.title: Tuning ef and M, and choosing an index

blocks.md: In production you tune one knob at query time and two at build time. The query-time knob is **ef** (`set_ef` in hnswlib, `efSearch` in Faiss, `hnsw.ef_search` in pgvector, the PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector column type and ANN indexes). Each value of ef gives one point on a recall versus speed curve, and you pick the cheapest point that meets your recall target and your latency target, usually stated as p99 latency: the time within which 99 percent of queries finish. ANN-Benchmarks (Aumuller, Bernhardsson and Faithfull), which runs many ANN libraries on the same datasets, evaluates libraries exactly this way: sweep parameters, then plot quality against speed.

blocks.title: Sweeping ef: recall vs work (our experiment)

scenes.caption: Recall@10 on 20,000 uniform 16-d vectors with the heuristic (M = 8, ef_construction = 64, 200 queries; the layer-0 code from lesson 4). Recall rises quickly then saturates: 61.2, 72.6, 84.2, 94.9, 98.8 percent.
Distance computations per query as a percent of brute force (20,000): 0.99, 1.29, 2.03, 3.43, 5.93 percent. Going from 94.9 to 98.8 percent recall costs 1.7x more work.

blocks.md: ef is one axis; M is the other. A larger M gives every node more links, so each expansion scores more neighbors (more work per step) but the graph is better connected (fewer misses). We swept both with hnswlib on SIFT10K: ef_construction = 200, one thread, 100 queries, recall@10. The speeds come from one run on this machine (an Apple Silicon Mac); a rerun moved individual values by up to about 9 percent, so read them only relative to each other.

blocks.title: M on SIFT10K with hnswlib (speeds from one run)

scenes.caption: Recall@10 (percent) at a fixed ef = 20: 83.3, 94.5, 98.2, 98.7. More links, fewer misses.
Thousands of queries per second at the same ef = 20: 132, 96, 70, 56. Every extra link is another distance per expanded node, so speed falls as M rises.

The question you actually face: thousands of queries per second at the cheapest ef that reaches 98 percent recall@10. M = 4 needs ef = 160 (20.9), M = 8 ef = 40 (54.2), M = 16 and M = 32 ef = 20 (70.4 and 56.2).

blocks.md: At a fixed target the curve has a sweet spot. With too few links (M = 4) the search needs a huge beam and ran 3.4x slower than M = 16 in this run (3.3x in a rerun); past the sweet spot extra links only add work (M = 32). Memory moves too: Faiss's guide gives HNSW's size as $d \times 4 + M \times 2 \times 4$ bytes per vector, so M = 32 adds 256 bytes of links to each 512-byte SIFT vector. On a larger or harder dataset the sweet spot shifts, so repeat the sweep on your own data.

blocks.code:
import hnswlib
import numpy as np

dim, n = 768, 10000
data = np.random.rand(n, dim).astype('float32')

index = hnswlib.Index(space='cosine', dim=dim)
index.init_index(max_elements=n, M=16, ef_construction=200)
index.add_items(data, np.arange(n))

index.set_ef(64)  # query-time beam width; must be >= k
labels, distances = index.knn_query(data[:5], k=10)
blocks.caption: hnswlib's Python API, following its README. Measure recall against brute force before trusting any setting.

blocks.md: Tune HNSW in this order: pick M for your data (12 to 48 is typical), set ef_construction high enough that build-time recall is near 1, then sweep ef at query time against brute-force ground truth until recall@k meets your target at acceptable latency.

HNSW is one of three families you can now reason about. Lesson 5 built IVF (partition, then probe a few cells) and lesson 6 built PQ (compress, estimate, re-rank). Side by side, their memory costs per 768-d vector are:

blocks.title: Bytes per 768-d vector by index type

scenes.caption: From the Faiss index table: Flat stores 4d = 3,072 bytes. IVF,Flat adds an 8-byte id (3,080). For HNSW we add the paper's average graph cost of about 151 bytes (3,223).

Compression changes the picture: 8-bit scalar quantization stores d + 8 = 776 bytes; PQ with 96 one-byte codes stores 96 + 8 = 104 bytes. At 10 million vectors that is about 1 GB instead of 30.7 GB for the raw floats.

blocks.md: Rules of thumb that follow from the mechanisms: HNSW gives strong recall versus speed, supports incremental inserts without training, but needs the full vectors and graph in RAM. IVF needs a training pass (k-means) and has a cheaper build and smaller overhead; pgvector's docs describe IVFFlat (IVF over full, flat vectors) as faster to build and smaller than HNSW but with a worse speed versus recall tradeoff. PQ is what you add when memory, not speed, is the binding constraint. Faiss can also combine them, for example HNSW over compressed codes (`IndexHNSWSQ`, `IndexHNSWPQ`).

blocks.caption: pgvector's HNSW index; m = 16 and ef_construction = 64 are the defaults its README lists, and <=> is cosine distance, 1 minus cosine similarity, so smaller means closer.

blocks.question: Your HNSW service hits 99 percent recall@10 but p99 latency is too high. Memory is fine and you cannot rebuild today. What is the right first move?
options: Lower M
Lower ef and re-measure recall vs latency
Lower ef_construction
Switch the metric from cosine to L2
blocks.explain: ef is the only knob that applies without a rebuild; M and ef_construction are fixed at build time. Our sweep shows recall saturates near the top, so a modest drop in ef can cut work substantially for a small recall loss.

blocks.question: You must index 1 billion 768-d vectors on machines with limited RAM. Which choice best fits the constraint?
options: HNSW,Flat, because it has the best recall versus speed
Brute force on GPUs, because it is exact
IVF with PQ codes, because each vector shrinks from 3,072 bytes to around 100
HNSW with a larger M, because more links mean less memory
blocks.explain: Raw float32 vectors alone would be about 3 TB, and HNSW,Flat needs them in RAM. IVF,PQ stores about m + 8 bytes per vector (about 104 GB with 96 codes). The lost recall is recovered by re-ranking a shortlist with full vectors kept on cheaper storage (lesson 6). A larger M increases memory, it does not reduce it.

lessons.title: Production scale: disk, rescoring, filters and updates

blocks.md: Everything so far assumed one index, in RAM, built once and queried without conditions. Real deployments break all three. A tiny example of the first: 200 million 768-d embeddings in float32 take 200,000,000 x 768 x 4 bytes = 614 GB, nearly ten times the RAM of a 64 GB machine. This lesson surveys the four constraints that decide real designs: indexes larger than RAM, compressed vectors with rescoring, filters, and updates. Each has its own course; here you get the mechanism and numbers to reason with.

**DiskANN** (Subramanya and others, NeurIPS 2019) keeps only PQ codes in RAM and puts the graph plus the full-precision vectors on SSD. The constraint is the SSD: a random read takes a few hundred microseconds, so the paper aims for fewer than ten round trips per query. Its beam search fetches the neighborhoods of the $W$ best unexpanded candidates (say 4 or 8) in one batch per round trip, steers with in-memory PQ distances, and re-ranks with the full vectors it read along the way. On the billion-vector SIFT1B dataset the paper reports more than 5,000 queries per second, under 3 ms mean latency and 95 percent+ 1-recall@1 (the single true nearest neighbor is found) on a 16-core machine with 64 GB of RAM.

blocks.title: One DiskANN query: PQ codes in RAM, graph and vectors on SSD

scenes.caption: Build the PQ distance table for the query (lesson 6). Every in-memory code can now be scored with a few lookups.
Round trip 1: read the records of the W = 4 best unexpanded candidates in one batch. Each record holds the node's full vector followed by its neighbor ids, so one read fetches both.
Score the newly found neighbors with PQ estimates from RAM; no disk access. The best of them become the next candidates.
Round trip 2, and so on. The paper aims for fewer than ten round trips per query, since each random SSD read takes a few hundred microseconds.
When the beam stops improving, re-rank: the full vectors that arrived with each record give exact distances for the final top k, with no extra reads.

blocks.md: Few round trips need a graph with few hops, which means long edges. DiskANN's graph, **Vamana**, is pruned with RobustPrune: the same diversity test as HNSW's heuristic from lesson 4, with one extra knob $\alpha \ge 1$. After keeping a neighbor $p^*$ for node $p$, a candidate $p'$ is discarded only if it is much closer to $p^*$ than to $p$. With $\alpha > 1$ fewer candidates are discarded, so more long-range edges survive and paths get shorter. The paper notes that HNSW and NSG (Navigating Spreading-out Graph, another single-layer proximity graph) implicitly use $\alpha = 1$.

blocks.tex: \text{discard } p' \iff \alpha \cdot d(p^*, p') \le d(p, p'), \qquad \alpha = 1: \text{HNSW's heuristic}, \quad \alpha > 1: \text{more long edges}
blocks.caption: RobustPrune, DiskANN Algorithm 2. With alpha = 1 this is lesson 4's test: keep a candidate only if it is closer to the new node than to every neighbor already kept.

blocks.md: Between all-in-RAM and on-SSD sits the common middle path: keep a **compressed** copy in the graph and **rescore** the top candidates with full vectors. Faiss composes it as `HNSW32,SQ8,RFlat` (HNSW over 8-bit scalar-quantized vectors, refined with flat vectors); pgvector's README shows binary quantization in an expression index, followed by an `ORDER BY` on the original vectors over the top 20. On SIFT10K with Faiss HNSW32 at ef = 40 we measured 100 percent recall@10 over float vectors (lesson 4's M = 16 graph gave 99.6), 98.9 percent over SQ8 (128 bytes instead of 512) and 100 percent for SQ8 with a 2x shortlist rescored.

blocks.title: Binary codes plus rescoring on SIFT10K

scenes.caption: 1-bit quantization: subtract the mean of the learning set, keep each dimension's sign (16 bytes per SIFT vector instead of 512), rank by Hamming distance, the number of differing bits. Alone it finds a third of the true top 10.

Rescoring Hamming shortlists of 40, 100 and 200 with exact distances: 58.6, 76.2 and 87.7 percent recall@10. The prerequisite's 384-bit codes kept 99.1 percent of nDCG@10, which forgives near-equal swaps; recall@10 counts exact neighbors.

blocks.prompt: You add `WHERE category = 'shoes'` to the pgvector HNSW query from lesson 7 (`ORDER BY embedding <=> ... LIMIT 10`). Shoes are 10 percent of the table, and hnsw.ef_search is 40. How many rows do you expect back from LIMIT 10?
blocks.reveal: About **4**, not 10. pgvector applies the filter *after* the index scan: the scan produces ef_search = 40 candidates, and on average 10 percent of them (4) match. pgvector's README gives exactly this example. The fixes are raising ef_search, enabling iterative index scans (`hnsw.iterative_scan`, which keeps scanning until enough rows match), or using a partial index (an index over only the rows matching a WHERE condition, such as one category) or partitioning (splitting the table into separate tables, each with its own index) for very selective filters.

blocks.md: Filtered vector search is the most common production surprise. Post-filtering an ANN result can return fewer than k rows and silently lower recall. Check whether your engine pre-filters (applies the filter first, then searches only matching rows), post-filters or scans iteratively. With post-filtering, expected matches = candidates x selectivity, the fraction of rows that pass the filter. hnswlib, for example, accepts a filter in knn_query that restricts results to allowed ids.

Post-filtering is one of several strategies, and which one wins depends on **selectivity**. We measured them on our layer-0 graph from lesson 4 (SIFT10K, M = 16, ef = 40) with a random attribute, against ground truth over the matching rows only:

- **Post-filter**: search normally, then drop non-matching results.
- **Walk matching nodes only**: never step onto a non-matching node. The subgraph of matching nodes falls apart as selectivity drops.
- **Walk all nodes, keep matching**: route through every node but admit only matching ones to the result list W. hnswlib's filter works this way.
- **Pre-filter**: find the matching rows first (for example with a B-tree on the attribute), then brute-force them. Exact, at one distance per matching row.

blocks.title: Recall@10 by filter strategy and selectivity (our graph, SIFT10K)

scenes.caption: 50 percent of rows match: all but the restricted walk stay near 100 percent. Distances per query: 530, 302, 819 and 4,953.

10 percent match: post-filter returns only 4.4 rows on average (as pgvector predicts) and the restricted walk strands itself. Walking all nodes keeps 100 percent but needs 2,001 distances; pre-filter needs 1,029.

1 percent match (101 rows): post-filter returns 0.4 rows; the restricted walk's entry has no matching neighbors. Walking all nodes still finds everything, at 5,315 distances, 53 times the 101 a pre-filter scan needs.

0.5 percent (58 rows): walking all nodes touches 9,228 of the 10,000 vectors. Below some selectivity, brute force over the matches is both exact and cheapest, so planners switch strategy by selectivity.

blocks.md: Two better tools. **ACORN** (Patel and others, 2024) builds HNSW with $M \cdot \gamma$ candidate neighbors per node instead of $M$, so that the subgraph of nodes passing a predicate stays navigable, then walks only matching nodes. With $\gamma = 1/s_{min}$ it serves selectivities down to $s_{min}$ and falls back to pre-filtering below that; the paper reports 2 to 1,000x higher throughput than prior methods at a fixed recall. pgvector offers **iterative index scans** that keep scanning until enough rows match (up to `hnsw.max_scan_tuples`), and suggests partial indexes for a few distinct filter values and partitioning for many. The pre-post-filtering course builds the full planner.

Two more operational facts. **Deletes**: Faiss documents that its HNSW index does not support removing vectors; hnswlib offers `mark_deleted`, which hides an element from results while keeping it in the graph for routing, and can later reuse the slot with `replace_deleted`. **Builds**: insertion cost scales like search, so the paper reports roughly $O(N \log N)$ construction for low-dimensional data, and hnswlib parallelizes `add_items` across threads.

Deletes also wear a graph down. FreshDiskANN (Singh and others, 2021) found that repeated delete and re-insert cycles made recall drop for HNSW, NSG and Vamana, because the graph grew sparser. Its fix is lazy: a deleted point goes on a DeleteList, searches still route through it but drop it from results (the same trick as hnswlib's `mark_deleted`), and once deletes reach about 1 to 10 percent of the index, a batch **consolidation** repairs the neighborhoods that pointed at them. Many databases instead write new data to fresh segments and merge or rebuild them periodically; the vector-database-internals course covers segments, tombstones and merges.

**Sharding.** When one machine is not enough, split the vectors across shards, send the query to every shard, let each return its own top $k$, and keep the best $k$ of the merged lists. Faiss's wiki uses the same pattern to search a dataset in slices with a running top-k heap. Recall then depends only on each shard's index: the merge loses nothing, because any vector in the global top $k$ is also in its own shard's top $k$.

**GPUs.** CAGRA (CUDA ANNS GRAph-based, Ootomo and others, 2023) builds a fixed-degree graph designed for GPU parallelism; its paper reports 33 to 77x the large-batch throughput of HNSW in the 90 to 95 percent recall range and 2.2 to 27x faster graph construction. The diskann-cagra course covers both systems.

**Benchmarks.** Compare indexes the way ANN-Benchmarks does: plot recall against queries per second over a parameter sweep, on the same data and queries. Big-ANN-Benchmarks (NeurIPS 2021) fixed the hardware and the throughput and compared recall@10 on billion-vector datasets: on BIGANN-1B the in-memory baseline (Faiss, 64 GB RAM, 10,000 queries per second) scored 0.634, and the SSD baseline (DiskANN, 64 GB RAM plus a 1 TB SSD, 1,500 queries per second) scored 0.949. The 2023 edition added filtered, out-of-distribution and sparse tracks, ranked by throughput at 90 percent recall@10, and a streaming track scored by recall after a fixed run of inserts, deletes and searches.

Pick the design by constraint. RAM decides between float vectors, compressed vectors with rescoring, and an SSD-resident graph. Selectivity decides between post-filter, filtered walk and pre-filter. Update rate decides between lazy deletes with consolidation and periodic rebuilds. Measure recall against brute force in each regime separately.

blocks.question: A query with a selective filter (1 percent of rows match) returns 0 or 1 results from an HNSW index with ef_search = 40. Which explanation fits?
options: The graph is disconnected, so the filtered rows are unreachable
The index post-filters about 40 candidates, so about 0.4 match on average
Cosine distance cannot be combined with WHERE clauses
ef_search is ignored when a filter is present
blocks.explain: With post-filtering, expected matches = candidates times selectivity = 40 x 0.01 = 0.4. Raise ef_search, enable iterative scans, or use a separate index or partition for that filter.

blocks.question: 200 million 768-d vectors, one machine with 64 GB of RAM and a fast SSD. 10 percent of queries carry a tenant filter that matches 0.5 percent of rows (1 million vectors). Which design fits?
options: HNSW over float32 vectors in RAM, post-filtering tenant queries with ef_search = 40
IVF with nprobe = 1 and no re-ranking, post-filtering tenant queries
An SSD-resident graph with 96-byte PQ codes in RAM (about 19 GB) and re-ranking from SSD, plus a separate index per tenant (partitioning) for filtered queries
Binary codes (96 bytes per vector) with no rescoring, post-filtering tenant queries
blocks.explain: Float32 vectors alone are 614 GB, so in-RAM HNSW cannot fit. 96-byte PQ codes take about 19 GB, and DiskANN-style search re-ranks from SSD. A 0.5 percent filter leaves post-filtering with about 40 x 0.005 = 0.2 rows, and brute force over 1 million 768-d rows reads about 3 GB per query, so a per-tenant index is the bounded option (even scanning its PQ codes is a million per query). Unrescored binary codes and nprobe = 1 give up too much recall.
